text:
Evidence supports testing mixed hard negatives, but does not establish gains on Electronics. A 2024 SASRec study compared six samplers over 20 repeats: adaptive-plus-mixed sampling achieved Amazon Beauty HR@10 of 2.33%, versus 1.44% for uniform and 1.64% for adaptive alone. However, adaptive alone achieved higher popularity-tail HR@10: 0.89% versus 0.27% for adaptive-plus-mixed. These are reported test results from validation-selected checkpoints, not RecHarness validation evidence; popularity-tail accuracy also differs from lower-tail score margins. [Study](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.17276v1)

Loss choice deserves a separate ablation. gSASRec links sampled BCE to overconfidence and proposes more negatives plus generalized BCE; its highlighted 41% improvement is NDCG@10 on Gowalla, not Electronics HR@10. Sampled softmax therefore remains a candidate requiring matched validation. NARec (2025) selects hard contrastive negatives from batch/global pools and augments them, reporting Beauty Recall@10 0.0877 versus 0.0863 for its strongest baseline. This supports investigating negative quality, but combines several changes and does not isolate sampled-softmax item ranking. [gSASRec](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/939), [NARec](https://ietresearch.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1049/aie2.70004)

False-negative handling is relevant: UFNRec uses teacher soft labels and consistency regularization for suspected false negatives rather than simply discarding them. Practical inference: compare uniform multi-negative sampled softmax against a mostly-uniform mixture with a small hard-negative fraction, masking known training positives and testing conservative downweighting of suspected false negatives. Select using pinned macro validation HR@10 across all four categories; improved margins alone are insufficient evidence. [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116)
